Campus CNRA:
In the Campus area vegetation consists of residential, commercial and institutional landscaping utilizing both native and exotic plant materials. Lawns, flower beds and shrubery are common throughout the area, but most impressive are the large mature trees to be found in yards and along streets. For example, a row of Sycamore is planted along Santa Clara Street between Sixth and Seventh Street, and along Sixth Street there are large California Pepper trees and Washington Palms, while massive Elms tower in front of John XXIII Senior enter along Fifth Street and San Fernando Street. Younger trees are to be found around the most recent development like the fast food restaurants on the northeast corner of Fourth and San Fernando Streets and the southwest corner of Sixth and Santa Clara Streets.
The mature trees and urban vegetation supports typical urban animal life. For example, Fox Squirrels inhabit the trees, while frequently observed birds include House Sparrow, House Finches, Starlings, Brown Towhee and Western Robins.
Gardner CNRA:
The Gardner area has landscaping typical of old residential areas with an impressive stock of healthy mature trees along many of the streets. Along Snyder Avenue there are two uniform rows of large Sycamores on each side of the street, while along the southside of the railroad tracks next to Fuller Avenue there is a row of Beefwoods. On West Virginia Street and Delmas Avenue around Biebrach Park there are Birch growing next to the sidewalk and interior to these is a row of Ash trees. In this park, near the recreation building, old Olive trees have been preserved and young Pines and Eucalyptus established. Sweet Gum trees have been frequently planted along streets and in front yards. Camphor trees are also common. Throughout the Gardner area are numerous huge old specimen trees such as the Coast Redwoods along Bird Avenue between Snyder and Brook Avenues, and perhaps the most impressive one is located at the bend in Bird Avenue. Large Blackwood Acacias tower at the north end of Illinois Avenue and on the southside of Highway 280.
Guadalupe River channel passes along the eastern side of the Gardner Area, crossing the southeast corner of the CNRA. The River channel is lined with Willows and some Poplars and Blue Elderberry. The animal life associated with Gardner is very similar to that of Olinder, because of the presence of riparian habitat along water course and because of the old mature trees and residential landscaping.
Mayfair CNRA:
The Mayfair area shows a wide range of variation in vegetation ranging from large mature trees like the Blue Gums near Mc Creery and Alum Rock Avenues to streets like Berkeley Way which have almost no trees at all.
